chief_complaint: progressive memory loss, getting lost in familiar neighborhood, repeating questions, and functional cognitive decline (Alzheimer Disease Evaluation)
hpi_details: 74F retired teacher brought to clinic by her adult daughter due to a 2-year insidious progression of memory problems. Daughter reports her mother has begun asking the same questions repeatedly within 15 minutes of being answered, frequently misplaces her keys and purse inside the refrigerator or oven, and forgets the names of close grandchildren. Two weeks ago, mother got lost while driving home from her local grocery store where she has shopped for 20 years and had to be brought home by police. Mother struggled recently to pay her monthly utility bills and balance her checkbook (`instrumental activities of daily living impairment`). Mother smiles pleasantly and insists her memory is `just fine for an old lady.` Denies hallucinations, tremor, shuffling gait, or sudden step-wise drops in ability.
ideas: patient pleasantly confused and unconcerned with her memory; daughter deeply worried and stressed about mother's safety living alone
concerns: daughter terrified mother has Alzheimer dementia and worried about leaving her alone with the stove on
expectations: wants memory testing, brain scan, and medications to slow down cognitive decline
social_hx: Retired high school teacher, lives alone in single-family home, non-smoker

clinical_knowledge.topic: Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes a comprehensive Family Medicine dementia and caregiver management plan, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive memory loss, getting lost in familiar neighborhood, repeating questions, and functional cognitive decline (Alzheimer Disease Evaluation)

Key HPI features: 74F retired teacher brought to clinic by her adult daughter due to a 2-year insidious progression of memory problems. Daughter reports her mother has begun asking the same questions repeatedly within 15 minutes of being answered, frequently misplaces her keys and purse inside the refrigerator or oven, and forgets the names of close grandchildren. Two weeks ago, mother got lost while driving home from her local grocery store where she has shopped for 20 years and had to be brought home by police. Mother struggled recently to pay her monthly utility bills and balance her checkbook (`instrumental activities of daily living impairment`). Mother smiles pleasantly and insists her memory is `just fine for an old lady.` Denies hallucinations, tremor, shuffling gait, or sudden step-wise drops in ability.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 72, BP 130/80. Neurological exam reveals normal cranial nerves, normal motor strength, normal bulk, normal reflexes without pathological signs, and a smooth, steady gait without shuffling, rigidity, or tremor (excluding Parkinsonian/Lewy Body dementia). Standardized Cognitive Assessment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score is 17/30 (scores <26 indicate impairment; patient loses points on delayed word recall 0/5, cube drawing, clock drawing hands placement, and orientation to date/day of week). Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score is 20/30 (Moderate Dementia). Reversible Dementia Laboratory Workup: Complete Blood Count, Comprehensive Metabolic Panel, Serum TSH (1.8 uIU/mL), and Serum Vitamin B12 (540 pg/mL) are all completely NORMAL (excluding hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, kidney/liver failure, or severe anemia). Brain MRI without contrast demonstrates moderate generalized cerebral atrophy with prominent, symmetric disproportionate volume loss and atrophy of the bilateral medial temporal lobes and Hippocampi (Scheltens Grade 3), without acute infarctions, subdural hematoma, or normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Current medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily, Atorvastatin 20mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vascular dementia (would have stepwise decline) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Getting lost while driving — an immediate safety issue requiring prompt action, not just monitoring.
management_principles: Comprehensive Family Medicine Dementia and Caregiver management plan

Pharmacotherapy: initiate first-line Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitor therapy: Donepezil (Aricept) starting at 5 mg PO QHS for 4 weeks, then titrating to 10 mg QHS (or Rivastigmine/Galantamine) to stabilize acetylcholine levels and modestly slow cognitive/behavioral decline

Since patient has moderate dementia (MMSE <20), co-prescribe Memantine (NMDA receptor antagonist, starting 5 mg daily titrating to 10 mg BID) for synergistic neuroprotection against glutamate excitotoxicity
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 74F presenting with 2-year insidious, progressive impairment in short-term episodic memory, topographic disorientation, and functional decline in Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs), diagnostic of Major Neurocognitive Disorder (Dementia).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 72, BP 130/80. Neurological exam reveals normal cranial nerves, normal motor strength, normal bulk, normal reflexes without pathological signs, and a smooth, steady gait without shuffling, rigidity, or tremor (excluding Parkinsonian/Lewy Body dementia). Standardized Cognitive Assessment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score is 17/30 (scores <26 indicate impairment; patient loses points on delayed word recall 0/5, cube drawing, clock drawing hands placement, and orientation to date/day of week). Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score is 20/30 (Moderate Dementia). Reversible Dementia Laboratory Workup: Complete Blood Count, Comprehensive Metabolic Panel, Serum TSH (1.8 uIU/mL), and Serum Vitamin B12 (540 pg/mL) are all completely NORMAL (excluding hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, kidney/liver failure, or severe anemia). Brain MRI without contrast demonstrates moderate generalized cerebral atrophy with prominent, symmetric disproportionate volume loss and atrophy of the bilateral medial temporal lobes and Hippocampi (Scheltens Grade 3), without acute infarctions, subdural hematoma, or normal pressure hydrocephalus.
reference_soap.assessment: Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer Disease, Moderate Stage (characterized by prominent hippocampal short-term memory loss and IADL impairment).
reference_soap.plan: Comprehensive Family Medicine Dementia and Caregiver management plan: 1. Pharmacotherapy: initiate first-line Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitor therapy: Donepezil (Aricept) starting at 5 mg PO QHS for 4 weeks, then titrating to 10 mg QHS (or Rivastigmine/Galantamine) to stabilize acetylcholine levels and modestly slow cognitive/behavioral decline. Since patient has moderate dementia (MMSE <20), co-prescribe Memantine (NMDA receptor antagonist, starting 5 mg daily titrating to 10 mg BID) for synergistic neuroprotection against glutamate excitotoxicity. 2. Safety & Functional mandates: immediate driving cessation counseling (file medical report with DMV given episode of getting lost and MoCA 17); recommend adult child assume Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare and Finances immediately; install stove auto-shutoff safety switches and medication lockboxes/blister packs managed by daughter. 3. Caregiver support: refer daughter to local Alzheimer's Association support groups and arrange social work evaluation for home health aide supervision or adult daycare transition.

learning_objectives: Administer and interpret validated cognitive screening tools (Montreal Cognitive Assessment MoCA and Mini-Mental State Examination MMSE) to quantify objective cognitive deficits across episodic memory, executive function, and visuospatial domains

Execute the essential primary care laboratory workup to exclude reversible causes of cognitive impairment and dementia phenocopies (Serum TSH to rule out hypothyroidism, Vitamin B12 and Folate to rule out nutritional deficiency, plus treponemal/non-treponemal syphilis serology (with CSF examination if reactive) to rule out neurosyphilis, CMP for hepatic/renal encephalopathy, and structural brain MRI/CT to rule out subdural hematoma, tumors, or normal pressure hydrocephalus)

Differentiate Alzheimer Disease (insidious progressive short-term memory loss, hippocampal atrophy) from Vascular Dementia (sudden step-wise decline associated with stroke/infarcts on MRI) and Dementia with Lewy Bodies (early visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, and Parkinsonian motor rigidity)

Prescribe evidence-based pharmacotherapy combining Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors (Donepezil/Rivastigmine) with NMDA receptor antagonists (Memantine) for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease, and coordinate critical caregiver safety interventions (driving cessation, financial power of attorney, home safety audits)

teaching.diagnosis: Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease
teaching.one_liner: A slow, progressive decline in memory and daily functioning — repeating questions, getting lost in familiar places, and struggling with finances — that the patient herself often minimizes, while family witnesses the real impact.
red_flags: Getting lost while driving — an immediate safety issue requiring prompt action, not just monitoring

must_ask.say: Has she been asking the same question repeatedly, even shortly after being answered?
Has she gotten lost anywhere familiar, like her usual grocery store?
Has she had trouble managing bills or her checkbook?
How many years has this been gradually getting worse?
What worries you most about her living alone?

history.answer: My daughter brought me in because she thinks my memory has been getting worse lately, though I honestly feel I am just getting older.
Of course, you have my full permission to speak with my daughter. She worries about me, so she can share anything she has noticed.
It has been coming on very slowly over the past two years, gradually getting a bit more noticeable rather than happening all at once.
My daughter says I repeat the same questions within fifteen minutes and misplace my purse or keys in strange places like the refrigerator.
I have had trouble recalling the names of my grandchildren recently, which is quite embarrassing for me.
Two weeks ago I got lost driving home from the grocery store I have shopped at for twenty years, and a police officer had to help me get home.
Sometimes I pause trying to find the right word during a conversation, but I can still explain what I mean.
Lately I have struggled to balance my checkbook and missed a couple of utility bills, so my daughter has stepped in to help.
I can still dress and bathe myself without trouble, but cooking full meals and keeping track of daily chores have become harder.
No, my alertness stays steady throughout the day without sudden drops, confusion, or periods of drowsiness.
No, my personality has not changed, and I have not had any angry outbursts, agitation, or inappropriate behavior.
No, I have never seen or heard things that were not really there, and I do not suspect anyone of taking my things.
I do not feel depressed or hopeless, and I still enjoy sitting in my garden and listening to music.
My sleep and appetite have been quite regular, with no trouble sleeping through the night or noticeable weight changes.
No, I have not had any shuffling, stiff movements, slowed walking, or hand tremors.
No, I have normal bladder control and have not had any accidents or sudden loss of urine.
No, I have not bumped my head, had any falls, or suffered from new or severe headaches.
No, I have never had one-sided weakness, numbness in my arms or legs, or slurred speech.
No, I have not been sensitive to the cold, nor have I noticed constipation, dry coarse skin, or swelling.
No, I have had no fever, chills, burning when urinating, or cough.
No, I have not started any new medications recently, and I do not take sleeping pills, sedatives, or strong painkillers.
I do not drink any alcohol at all, and I have never been a drinker.
I have had high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol for several years, but never diabetes, heart disease, or a stroke.
My daughter is terrified that I might leave the stove on while living alone, and after getting lost, she insisted that I stop driving.
I feel my memory is just fine for an old woman, but my daughter is terrified that I have Alzheimer's disease and wants me tested.
Aside from high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol, I have had no major medical conditions.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy as a teenager, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams daily for blood pressure and atorvastatin 20 milligrams daily for cholesterol, with no other pills or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I am a retired high school English teacher and live alone in my single-family home since my husband passed away.
My mother lived into her late eighties and had some mild forgetfulness, but no one in my family had early dementia.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
Pleasant elderly woman who is neatly groomed, calm, and smiling pleasantly without acute distress.
MoCA score is 17/30 with loss of points on delayed word recall (0/5), clock drawing, cube drawing, and date orientation; MMSE score is 20/30.
Cranial nerves II through XII are intact with normal visual fields, symmetric facial movements, and normal extraocular motility.
Normal muscle tone and 5/5 motor strength in all four extremities without cogwheel rigidity, spasticity, or focal weakness.
No resting, postural, or action tremors observed in any extremity.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric throughout with bilateral downward plantar responses and no primitive release reflexes.
Intact light touch, pinprick, and vibration sensation symmetrically across all distal extremities.
Gait is smooth, upright, and steady without shuffling, hesitation, or ataxia, and Romberg test is negative.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules or thyromegaly.
Skin is warm, elastic, and normal in texture without coarseness, cool dryness, or myxedema.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2 sounds, and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal breath sounds and no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
